title: Smooth buttercream finish
subtitle: a flat, clean surface on a frosted layer cake using a bench scraper
excerpt: A smooth buttercream finish uses a straight-edged bench scraper held lightly against a rotating cake to level the outer coat in one steady pass. The cake needs a firm crumb coat as the base and buttercream at room temperature for the outer coat. The finish improves with each pass as the surface evens out.
sourceNotes: Smooth buttercream technique standard in British and American professional cake-decorating from the 1970s onward. The bench scraper method is the home-baking adaptation of the professional metal side scraper.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin first layer of buttercream applied to a filled layer cake to trap loose crumbs before the final decorative coat.

content.text: A smooth buttercream finish is the technique for getting a flat, even surface on a frosted layer cake. A bench scraper is held still against the side of the cake while the turntable rotates underneath, and the scraper shaves the buttercream level. The key step is a firm
The buttercream for the outer coat must be at room temperature. Cold buttercream tears; very soft buttercream moves after each pass. The right temperature gives a surface that holds the scraper mark.
Set the chilled, crumb-coated cake on the turntable. Load a generous amount of buttercream onto the top with a spatula and push it out to the edges, letting a little overhang.
Apply buttercream to the sides with the spatula in rough, overlapping patches. It does not need to look even at this stage. Aim for at least 5 to 6 mm of coverage all around.

Hold the bench scraper vertically against the side of the cake. The bottom edge rests lightly on the turntable board or the surface of the cake board. Keep the scraper still and spin the turntable in one full rotation.

Scrape the excess off the scraper back into the bowl. Repeat the scraper pass two or three times, adding a little fresh buttercream to fill any thin patches. Each pass takes off a little more and the surface gets flatter.
Use the spatula to pull the lip of buttercream that has built up on the top edge inward, drawing it toward the centre. Work in short sweeps, always pulling toward the middle.
Add a thin layer of fresh buttercream to the top and smooth it flat with the spatula held parallel to the surface. One long even stroke across the full diameter is better than many short strokes.
Run the hot spatula across the surface of the top once to melt and even out any remaining ridges.

attrs.problem: Surface tearing when the scraper passes over it
attrs.avoid: Avoid cold buttercream for the outer coat; it drags and tears under the scraper.
attrs.fix: Leave the buttercream out until it is soft but still holds its shape. If it has been in the fridge, beat briefly with a spatula until spreadable.

attrs.problem: Lines and ridges still visible after multiple passes
attrs.avoid: Avoid pressing the scraper hard; pressure creates marks rather than removing them.
attrs.fix: Hold the scraper lightly and add a thin fresh coat of buttercream over the problem area before the next pass. Let the rotation do the work.

attrs.avoid: Avoid pulling the top lip outward; this creates a rounded rather than a square edge.
attrs.fix: Use a small amount of fresh buttercream on the edge and draw the spatula inward in short strokes from the edge toward the centre.
